# Introduction
This lab examines whether people with higher Extraversion scores are more likely to endorse the Big Five item “Know how to comfort others” (A3).
I expected a positive association because more outgoing people may have more opportunities to respond to others’ distress, which could be associated with greater confidence in knowing how to comfort someone. Because the item has ordered response categories, I used a cumulative logit model to estimate how the distribution of responses varies with Extraversion.

# Workflow
**1.** Score the Big Five subscales, prepare A3 as an ordered outcome, and centre Extraversion in the analysis sample.
**2.** Describe the A3 responses and calculate the observed cumulative probabilities, odds, and log-odds.
**3.** Fit and compare a threshold-only model and a model with Extraversion, then check the proportional-odds assumption.
**4.** Interpret the shared odds ratio and visualize predicted response probabilities across the observed range of Extraversion.

# Research Question and Prediction
**Question.** Is Extraversion associated with higher endorsement of “Know how to comfort others”?
**Prediction.** I expect people with higher Extraversion scores to be more likely to endorse the item. People who are more socially outgoing may have more opportunities to respond to others’ distress, which could be associated with greater confidence in knowing how to comfort someone.

# Dataset
**Note**
The bfi data set and items should not be confused with the BFI (Big Five Inventory) of Oliver John and colleagues (John, O. P., Donahue, E. M., & Kentle, R. L. (1991). The Big Five Inventory–Versions 4a and 54. Berkeley, CA: University of California,Berkeley, Institute of Personality and Social Research.)

**Source**
The items are from the ipip (Goldberg, 1999). The data are from the SAPA project (Revelle, Wilt and Rosenthal, 2010) , collected Spring, 2010 ( https://www.sapa-project.org/).
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/psych/html/bfi.html

# Method
# Part 1.Load packages and prepare the setup
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(psych)
library(ordinal)
library(ggeffects)
library(broom)
library(gt)

fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 0.1)
p_label <- function(p) {
  if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste0("= ", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
}

response_levels <- c(
  "Very inaccurate", "Moderately inaccurate", "Slightly inaccurate",
  "Slightly accurate", "Moderately accurate", "Very accurate"
)

keys <- list(
  Agreeableness     = c("-A1", "A2", "A3", "A4", "A5"),
  Conscientiousness = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "-C4", "-C5"),
  Extraversion      = c("-E1", "-E2", "E3", "E4", "E5"),
  Neuroticism       = c("N1", "N2", "N3", "N4", "N5"),
  Openness          = c("O1", "-O2", "O3", "O4", "-O5")
)

item_names <- sub("^-", "", unlist(keys, use.names = FALSE))
raw_bfi <- read_excel("bfi.xlsx")

items <- raw_bfi |>
  select(all_of(item_names)) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

stopifnot(all(unlist(items) %in% c(1:6, NA)))

scores <- psych::scoreItems(
  keys, items, totals = FALSE, min = 1, max = 6,
  missing = TRUE, impute = "none"
)$scores

lab_data <- tibble(
  A3 = factor(items$A3, levels = 1:6,
              labels = response_levels, ordered = TRUE),
  extra = if_else(
    complete.cases(items[paste0("E", 1:5)]),
    scores[, "Extraversion"],
    NA_real_
  ),
  dominant = factor(
    colnames(scores)[max.col(scores, ties.method = "first")],
    levels = names(keys)
  )
) |>
  drop_na(A3, extra, dominant) |>
  mutate(extra_c = extra - mean(extra))

extra_mean <- mean(lab_data$extra)
```

The analysis included `r format(nrow(lab_data), big.mark = ",")` participants. Extraversion was scored as the mean of its five items after reverse-scoring the first two items. The mean before centring was `r fmt(extra_mean)`.

# Part 2. Examine the Outcomes
## 2.1 A3 Response Frequency Table
```{r}
a3_counts <- lab_data |>
  count(A3, .drop = FALSE) |>
  mutate(p = n / sum(n))

a3_counts |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(A3 = "Response to A3", n = "Count", p = "Proportion") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = p, decimals = 1)
```
All response categories were represented and retained. The least frequent category was *Very inaccurate* (*n* = `r min(a3_counts$n)`,
`r pct(min(a3_counts$p))`).


## 2.2 Bar Chart of A3 Responses
```{r}
ggplot(a3_counts, aes(A3, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#376D80", width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(13), drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Participants") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Responses clustered toward the accurate end of the scale, with *Moderately accurate* as the most common response (`r pct(max(a3_counts$p))`).

## 2.3 Jittered Dot Plot of A3 Responses by Extraversion
```{r}
ggplot(lab_data, aes(extra, as.integer(A3))) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.06, height = 0.14, seed = 9041),
    alpha = 0.22, colour = "#376D80"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6, labels = response_levels) +
  labs(x = "Extraversion (subscale mean)", y = "Response to A3") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Each response falls into an ordered category, so the model estimates a probability for each of the six response options.

## 2.4 Bar Chart of Dominant Traits
```{r}
lab_data |>
  count(dominant, .drop = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(dominant, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#77618A", width = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Participants", y = "Highest-scoring trait") +
  theme_minimal()

obs_tab <- a3_counts |>
  mutate(
    cumulative_p = cumsum(n) / sum(n),
    cumulative_odds = if_else(
      row_number() < n(), cumulative_p / (1 - cumulative_p), NA_real_
    ),
    cumulative_logit = if_else(
      row_number() < n(), qlogis(cumulative_p), NA_real_
    )
  )
```
Agreeableness was the most common highest-scoring trait, and Neuroticism was the least common. The bars are sorted by frequency, while the trait categories themselves have no inherent order.


# Part 3. Cumulative Probabilities
## 3.1 Observed Cumulative Probabilities, Odds, and Log-Odds
```{r}
obs_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    A3 = "Response to A3", n = "Count", p = "P(Y = j)",
    cumulative_p = "P(Y ≤ j)", cumulative_odds = "Odds of Y ≤ j",
    cumulative_logit = "Log-odds of Y ≤ j"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(p, cumulative_p), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(cumulative_odds, cumulative_logit), decimals = 2) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")
```
About `r pct(obs_tab$cumulative_p[3])` of participants selected *Slightly inaccurate* or a lower category. The six response categories yield five cumulative cutpoints because the last category includes everyone. The probability of responding above that category is zero, so its cumulative odds and log-odds have no finite value.

#Part 4. Fit and Interpret Cumulative Logit Models
## 4.1 Fit the Threshold-Only and Extraversion Models
The A3 response categories have a natural order, and the distances between adjacent categories may differ. A cumulative logit model uses the order of the responses to estimate the probability of responding at or below each cutpoint.
```{r}
stopifnot(all(a3_counts$n > 0))
m0 <- clm(A3 ~ 1, data = lab_data, link = "logit")
m1 <- clm(A3 ~ extra_c, data = lab_data, link = "logit")

summary(m1)
```
About `r pct(obs_tab$cumulative_p[3])` of participants selected *Slightly inaccurate* or a lower category. The six response categories yield five cumulative cutpoints because the last category includes everyone. The probability of responding above that category is zero, so its cumulative odds and log-odds have no finite value.


## 4.2 Interpret the Thresholds at Average Extraversion
```{r}
th <- m1$alpha
b <- coef(m1)[["extra_c"]]
cum_avg <- plogis(th)
cat_avg <- diff(c(0, cum_avg, 1))
endorse_avg <- 1 - cum_avg[3]

tibble(
  Response = response_levels,
  Threshold = c(unname(th), NA_real_),
  `P(Y ≤ j)` = c(unname(cum_avg), 1),
  `P(Y = j)` = cat_avg
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Threshold, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(`P(Y ≤ j)`, `P(Y = j)`), decimals = 1) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")
```

Centring sets zero to the sample mean of Extraversion, so the thresholds describe a participant with an average score. This changes the reference point and leaves the slope unchanged. At average Extraversion, the most likely response was *`r response_levels[which.max(cat_avg)]`* (`r pct(max(cat_avg))`), and the predicted probability of responding *Slightly accurate* or higher was `r pct(endorse_avg)`.

## 4.3 Compare M0 Thresholds with Observed Cumulative Log-Odds
```{r}
tibble(
  Cutpoint = names(m0$alpha),
  Observed_logit = head(obs_tab$cumulative_logit, -1),
  M0_threshold = unname(m0$alpha)
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Observed_logit, M0_threshold), decimals = 3)
```
The M0 thresholds match the observed cumulative log-odds because M0 has no predictors and describes the overall response distribution. The M1 thresholds describe the predicted distribution at average Extraversion.

#Part 5. Compare the Models and Interpret the Slope
## 5.1 Likelihood-Ratio Test
```{r}
lrt <- anova(m0, m1)
lrt
lr_stat <- lrt$LR.stat[2]
lr_df <- lrt$df[2]
lr_p <- lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
```
Adding Extraversion improved model fit relative to the threshold-only model, χ²(`r lr_df`) = `r fmt(lr_stat)`, *p* `r p_label(lr_p)`.

## 5.2 AIC Comparison and Model Selection
```{r}
lr_stat <- lrt$LR.stat[2]
lr_df <- lrt$df[2]
lr_p <- lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
aic_difference <- abs(AIC(m0) - AIC(m1))

tibble(
  Model = c("M0: Thresholds only", "M1: Extraversion"),
  Parameters = c(length(coef(m0)), length(coef(m1))),
  `Log-likelihood` = c(as.numeric(logLik(m0)), as.numeric(logLik(m1))),
  AIC = c(AIC(m0), AIC(m1))
) |>
  mutate(`ΔAIC` = AIC - min(AIC)) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(`Log-likelihood`, AIC, `ΔAIC`), decimals = 2)
```
M1 had a lower AIC than M0 (ΔAIC = `r fmt(aic_difference)`). Both the likelihood-ratio test and AIC favoured M1, so I carried it forward to the proportional-odds check.

## 5.3 Interpret the Extraversion Slope on the Latent Scale
```{r}
middle_width <- mean(diff(th)[2:3])
fraction_of_middle_category <- abs(b) / middle_width
```
A one-point increase in Extraversion was associated with an upward shift of `r fmt(b)` units on the latent response scale. This shift was about `r pct(fraction_of_middle_category)` of the average width of the two middle response categories on that scale.

# Part 6. Check the Proportional-Odds Assumption
## 6.1 Likelihood-Ratio Test for Proportional Odds
```{r}
po_test <- nominal_test(m1)
po_test

po_lrt <- po_test["extra_c", "LRT"]
po_df  <- po_test["extra_c", "Df"]
po_p   <- po_test["extra_c", "Pr(>Chi)"]
```
Allowing the Extraversion slope to vary across cutpoints did not significantly improve fit, χ²(`r po_df`) = `r fmt(po_lrt)`, *p* `r p_label(po_p)`. I retained the proportional-odds model.

## 6.2 Estimate Threshold-Specific Odds Ratios for the Plot
```{r}
m_nom <- clm(A3 ~ 1, nominal = ~ extra_c, data = lab_data, link = "logit")

if (po_p < .05) {
  print(anova(m1, m_nom))
}

nom_coefs <- coef(m_nom)
nom_terms <- paste0(names(th), ".extra_c")
stopifnot(all(nom_terms %in% names(nom_coefs)))

nom_est <- nom_coefs[nom_terms]
nom_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(m_nom)))[nom_terms]
z_95 <- qnorm(.975)

threshold_or <- tibble(
  Threshold = names(th),
  OR = exp(-nom_est),
  low = exp(-nom_est - z_95 * nom_se),
  high = exp(-nom_est + z_95 * nom_se),
  Model = "Threshold-specific"
)

if (po_p < .05) {
  threshold_or |>
    select(-Model) |>
    gt() |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(OR, low, high), decimals = 2) |>
    print()
}
```


# Part 7. Interpret Odds Ratios and Predicted Probabilities
## 7.1 Shared Cumulative Odds Ratio
```{r}
or_tab <- tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "extra_c", coef.type == "location")

odds_change <- abs(or_tab$estimate - 1)
odds_direction <- if (or_tab$estimate >= 1) "higher" else "lower"
```
Each one-point increase in Extraversion was associated with `r pct(odds_change)` `r odds_direction` odds of responding above any given cutpoint, OR = `r fmt(or_tab$estimate)`, `r scales::percent(.95)` CI [`r fmt(or_tab$conf.low)`, `r fmt(or_tab$conf.high)`], *p* `r p_label(or_tab$p.value)`.

## 7.2 Predicted Probability of Endorsing the Item
# Use equal one-point steps within the observed range.
```{r}
raw_range <- range(lab_data$extra)
score_grid <- seq(ceiling(raw_range[1]), floor(raw_range[2]), by = 1)

prob_tab <- tibble(
  Extraversion = score_grid,
  Probability = plogis(b * (Extraversion - extra_mean) - th[3]),
  Odds = Probability / (1 - Probability),
  `Odds ratio vs previous score` = Odds / lag(Odds),
  `Change vs previous score (pp)` = 100 * (Probability - lag(Probability))
)

prob_tab |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = Probability, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Odds, `Odds ratio vs previous score`,
                `Change vs previous score (pp)`),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")
```
The predicted probability of responding *Slightly accurate* or higher rose from `r pct(first(prob_tab$Probability))` to `r pct(last(prob_tab$Probability))` across the observed Extraversion range. The odds multiplied by `r fmt(or_tab$estimate)` at each step, while
the probability increased by fewer percentage points as it approached one.

## 7.3 Predicted Probabilities for All Response Categories
```{r}
#| label: fig-category-probabilities
#| fig-cap: "Predicted response probabilities for the comfort item from the proportional-odds model."

pred <- ggpredict(m1, terms = "extra_c [all]") |>
  as.data.frame()

category <- as.character(pred$response.level)
category_index <- match(category, as.character(seq_along(response_levels)))

pred <- pred |>
  mutate(
    Extraversion = x + extra_mean,
    Response = factor(
      coalesce(response_levels[category_index], category),
      levels = response_levels
    )
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(pred$Response), !anyNA(pred$predicted))

ggplot(pred, aes(Extraversion, predicted, fill = Response, group = Response)) +
  geom_area(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  labs(
    x = "Extraversion (subscale mean)",
    y = "Predicted probability",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
As Extraversion increased, the predicted response distribution shifted toward higher categories, with *Very accurate* becoming more likely.

## 7.4 Shared and Threshold-Specific Odds Ratios
```{r}
#| label: fig-odds-ratios
#| fig-cap: "Shared and threshold-specific cumulative odds ratios for Extraversion."

bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Threshold = "Shared (proportional odds)",
    OR = or_tab$estimate,
    low = or_tab$conf.low,
    high = or_tab$conf.high,
    Model = "Shared"
  ),
  threshold_or
) |>
  mutate(Threshold = fct_rev(fct_inorder(Threshold))) |>
  ggplot(aes(OR, Threshold, colour = Model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio for responding above the threshold",
       y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
The threshold-specific odds ratios clustered around the shared estimate, and all confidence intervals lay above one. This pattern was consistent
with the likelihood-ratio test and supported retaining a common slope across cutpoints.


# Part 8. Findings and Limitations
I fit a cumulative logit model predicting responses to “Know how to comfort others” from mean-centred Extraversion (*N* = `r format(nobs(m1), big.mark = ",")`). The smallest response category contained `r min(a3_counts$n)` observations, and all categories were retained. Adding Extraversion improved fit over the threshold-only model, χ²(`r lr_df`) = `r fmt(lr_stat)`, *p* `r p_label(lr_p)`, and reduced AIC by `r fmt(aic_difference)`. Each one-point increase in Extraversion was associated with `r pct(odds_change)` higher odds of responding above any given cutpoint, *OR* = `r fmt(or_tab$estimate)`, `r scales::percent(.95)` CI [`r fmt(or_tab$conf.low)`, `r fmt(or_tab$conf.high)`], *p* `r p_label(or_tab$p.value)`. Allowing the slope to vary across cutpoints did not significantly improve fit, χ²(`r po_df`) = `r fmt(po_lrt)`, *p* `r p_label(po_p)`, so I retained the proportional-odds model.

The predicted probability of responding *Slightly accurate* or higher was `r pct(dplyr::first(prob_tab$Probability))` at an Extraversion score
of `r dplyr::first(prob_tab$Extraversion)` and `r pct(dplyr::last(prob_tab$Probability))` at a score of `r dplyr::last(prob_tab$Extraversion)` (see @fig-category-probabilities). A3 measures how people describe their ability to comfort others, and the analysis did not assess how they respond when someone is distressed. Both measures were self-reported, and the observational design limits the conclusion to an association. Within these limits, the results supported the prediction that higher Extraversion would be associated with stronger endorsement of the item.
